Home› Health A to Z› Type 2 diabetes

Health A to Z

Conditions, symptoms and treatments, including what to do and when to get help

Browse conditions by letter

ABCDEF GHIJKL MNOPQR STUVWX YZ

Contents

  • Overview
  • Symptoms
  • Causes
  • Getting diagnosed
  • Treatment
  • Living with Type 2 diabetes

Overview — Type 2 diabetes

Type 2 diabetes is a common condition that causes the level of sugar (glucose) in the blood to become too high. It's caused by problems with a chemical in the body called insulin.

It's often linked to being overweight or inactive, or having a family history of type 2 diabetes. Without treatment, it can cause serious problems with your eyes, heart and nerves.

What is HbA1c?

HbA1c (sometimes called glycated haemoglobin) is a measure of your average blood glucose level over the past 2 to 3 months. A blood test result of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or above usually means you have type 2 diabetes.

Blood glucose is the main sugar found in your blood and your body's primary source of energy.

Symptoms

Many people have type 2 diabetes without realising. This is because symptoms do not necessarily make you feel unwell.

Symptoms of type 2 diabetes include:

  • peeing more than usual, especially at night
  • feeling thirsty all the time
  • feeling very tired
  • losing weight without trying to
  • itching around your penis or vagina, or repeatedly getting thrush
  • cuts or wounds taking longer to heal
  • blurred vision

Urgent advice: Contact 111 if:

  • you have symptoms of type 2 diabetes
  • your blood sugar level is consistently higher than 11 mmol/L
  • you have signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), such as feeling or being sick, deep or fast breathing, breath that smells fruity, or feeling very drowsy

DKA is a serious problem that needs urgent treatment in hospital.

Causes

Type 2 diabetes happens when your body does not make enough insulin, or the insulin it makes does not work properly. This is known as insulin resistance.

You're more at risk of developing type 2 diabetes if you:

  • are over 40 (or 25 for south Asian people)
  • have a close relative with diabetes (such as a parent, brother or sister)
  • are overweight or obese
  • are of Asian, African-Caribbean or black African origin (even if you were born in the UK)

Getting diagnosed

See a GP if you have any of the symptoms of type 2 diabetes, or you're worried you may have a higher risk of getting it.

You'll need a blood test, which you may have to go to your local health centre for if it cannot be done at your GP surgery.

The Diabetes UK risk tool

You can use the Diabetes UK Know Your Risk tool to check your risk of type 2 diabetes. It only takes a few minutes and could be the most important thing you do today.

Treatment

There's no cure for type 2 diabetes, but treatment can help keep your blood sugar levels under control.

Treatment usually involves:

  • healthy eating — eating a wide range of foods, including some carbohydrates, fruit and vegetables
  • regular physical activity
  • losing weight if you're overweight
  • medicine — usually tablets such as metformin

Your GP may refer you to the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme if you're at high risk of developing type 2 diabetes. The programme can help you make lasting lifestyle changes.

Important

If you're prescribed metformin, do not stop taking it without speaking to a doctor first — even if you feel better. Stopping your medicine suddenly can cause your blood sugar to rise.

Living with Type 2 diabetes

Managing type 2 diabetes is mainly down to you. These daily steps can help you stay well:

  1. Eat a balanced diet — include vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, beans, pulses, nuts, fish, eggs and dairy. Cut down on sugar, salt and red or processed meat.
  2. Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity every week — such as brisk walking, swimming or cycling.
  3. Take your medicine exactly as prescribed and never skip doses.
  4. Check your feet every day for cuts, blisters or numbness, and report any changes to your GP or podiatrist.
  5. Attend your annual diabetic eye screening appointment to check for diabetic retinopathy.
  6. Stop smoking if you smoke — ask your GP about free NHS Stop Smoking support.

Call 999 if you or someone you know is unconscious or having a seizure

Severe low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) or DKA can be life-threatening and need emergency treatment.

More resources

  • NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme
  • Diabetes UK — support and information
  • Find a local diabetes specialist nurse

Home› Medicines A to Z› Amoxicillin

Amoxicillin

Antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections

Brand names
Amoxil, Amix
Type of medicine
Penicillin antibiotic
Prescription only
Yes — prescription only

Contents

  1. About amoxicillin
  2. Who can take it
  3. How and when to take it
  4. Side effects
  5. Pregnancy and breastfeeding
  6. Interactions
  7. Common questions

About amoxicillin

Amoxicillin is a penicillin antibiotic. It's used to treat bacterial infections, such as chest infections (including pneumonia) and dental abscesses.

It can also be used together with other antibiotics and medicines to treat stomach ulcers caused by H. pylori infection.

Key facts

  • Take amoxicillin at evenly spaced times throughout the day.
  • Common side effects include feeling sick (nausea) and diarrhoea.
  • Finish the full course of medicine even if you feel better.
  • Liquid amoxicillin can stain your teeth — this does not last and is removed by brushing.
  • Amoxicillin is generally safe to take during pregnancy and while breastfeeding.

Who can and cannot take amoxicillin

Amoxicillin can be taken by adults, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, and children.

Amoxicillin is not suitable for everyone. Tell your doctor before starting the medicine if you:

  • have ever had an allergic reaction to amoxicillin or any other medicine
  • have liver or kidney problems
  • have recently had, or are about to have, any vaccinations

How and when to take amoxicillin

The usual dose of amoxicillin capsules is 250mg to 500mg taken 3 times a day. The dose may be lower for children.

  1. Swallow capsules whole with a drink of water. Do not chew or break them.
  2. Space your doses evenly throughout the day — try to take them every 8 hours.
  3. You can take the medicine with or without food. For liquid medicine, use the plastic syringe or spoon that comes with it.
  4. Carry on taking the medicine until you've completed the course, even if you feel better. Stopping early can make the infection come back.
  5. If you forget a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless your next dose is due in less than 4 hours, in which case skip the missed dose.
⚠ Important

Allergic reactions — when to call 999

In rare cases, amoxicillin can cause a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis).

Call 999 or go to A&E now if:

  • your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen
  • you're breathing very fast or struggling to breathe (you may become very wheezy or feel like you're choking)
  • your throat feels tight or you're struggling to swallow
  • your skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale
  • you suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy
  • someone faints and cannot be woken up
  • a child is limp, floppy or not responding like they normally do

You or the person who's unwell may also have a rash that's swollen, raised, itchy, blistered or peeling.

Side effects

Like all medicines, amoxicillin can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them.

Common side effects

These common side effects of amoxicillin happen in more than 1 in 100 people. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if these side effects bother you or do not go away:

  • feeling sick (nausea)
  • diarrhoea
  • thrush (a yeast infection in the vagina, mouth or under foreskin)
  • headache
  • mild skin rash

Serious side effects

It happens rarely, but some people have serious side effects after taking amoxicillin.

Call a doctor or call 111 straight away if you get:

  • diarrhoea (sometimes with stomach cramps) that contains blood or mucus — if you have severe diarrhoea for more than 4 days
  • pale poo with dark pee, yellowing of the whites of your eyes or your skin (jaundice)
  • bruising or skin discolouration
  • joint or muscle pain that comes on after 2 days of taking the medicine
  • a skin rash with circular red patches

Pregnancy and breastfeeding

Amoxicillin is generally considered safe to take during pregnancy and while breastfeeding.

For more information about how amoxicillin can affect you and your baby, read the leaflet about amoxicillin on the Best Use of Medicines in Pregnancy (BUMPS) website.

Cautions with other medicines

There are some medicines that may affect how amoxicillin works, or that amoxicillin itself may affect.

Medicines that interact with amoxicillin

MedicineEffect of the interaction
Methotrexate (used to treat arthritis and psoriasis)Amoxicillin can increase methotrexate levels, raising the risk of side effects.
Warfarin (a blood thinner)May increase the risk of bleeding. Extra INR monitoring may be needed.
The contraceptive pillIf you experience sickness or diarrhoea, the pill may not work properly — use extra contraception.
Allopurinol (used for gout)Taking this with amoxicillin may increase the chance of an allergic skin rash.
Other antibiotics (e.g. tetracyclines, chloramphenicol)May reduce the effectiveness of amoxicillin.
Typhoid vaccine (oral)Amoxicillin can stop the typhoid vaccine working — tell your nurse or doctor.

Tell your doctor or pharmacist if you're taking any other medicines, including herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements.

Common questions

How long does amoxicillin take to work?

For most infections, you should feel better within a few days. It's very important you keep taking amoxicillin until your course is finished.

Will it affect my contraception?

Amoxicillin does not stop the contraceptive pill working. However, if it makes you sick or gives you severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, your contraceptive pills may not protect you from pregnancy.

Can I drink alcohol with it?

Yes, you can drink alcohol while taking amoxicillin.

Get urgent help

When to get help straight away

For a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), call 999 or go to A&E immediately.

999

About amoxicillin

Amoxicillin is a penicillin antibiotic. It's used to treat bacterial infections, such as chest infections (including pneumonia) and dental abscesses.

It can also be used together with other antibiotics and medicines to treat stomach ulcers caused by H. pylori infection.

Key facts

  • Take amoxicillin at evenly spaced times throughout the day.
  • Common side effects include feeling sick (nausea) and diarrhoea.
  • Finish the full course of medicine even if you feel better.
  • Liquid amoxicillin can stain your teeth — this does not last and is removed by brushing.
  • Amoxicillin is generally safe to take during pregnancy and while breastfeeding.

Who can and cannot take amoxicillin

Amoxicillin can be taken by adults, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, and children.

Amoxicillin is not suitable for everyone. Tell your doctor before starting the medicine if you:

  • have ever had an allergic reaction to amoxicillin or any other medicine
  • have liver or kidney problems
  • have recently had, or are about to have, any vaccinations

How and when to take amoxicillin

The usual dose of amoxicillin capsules is 250mg to 500mg taken 3 times a day. The dose may be lower for children.

  1. Swallow capsules whole with a drink of water. Do not chew or break them.
  2. Space your doses evenly throughout the day — try to take them every 8 hours.
  3. You can take the medicine with or without food. For liquid medicine, use the plastic syringe or spoon that comes with it.
  4. Carry on taking the medicine until you've completed the course, even if you feel better. Stopping early can make the infection come back.
  5. If you forget a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless your next dose is due in less than 4 hours, in which case skip the missed dose.

  • your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen
  • you're breathing very fast or struggling to breathe (you may become very wheezy or feel like you're choking)
  • your throat feels tight or you're struggling to swallow
  • your skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale
  • you suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy

Home› Mental health

Get urgent help for mental health

If you or someone you know is in a mental health crisis, help is available right now — 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

  • Call Samaritans free on 116 123 — open 24/7
  • Text SHOUT to 85258 — free, anonymous text support
  • Call 111 and select the mental health option
  • If life is at risk, call 999 or go to A&E

Mental health

Advice, support and where to get help for your mental wellbeing.

Mental health conditions

Information on common mental health conditions, including symptoms, causes, treatments and where to get help.

▲

Depression

Find out about the symptoms of depression and the different treatments available.

Read more
◐

Anxiety

Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is a long-term condition that causes you to feel anxious about a wide range of situations.

Read more
◯

OCD

Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) is a common mental health condition where a person has obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviours.

Read more
+

PTSD

Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is an anxiety disorder caused by very stressful, frightening or distressing events.

Read more
◆

Eating disorders

Information about anorexia, bulimia, binge eating disorder and other eating problems.

Read more
♡

Postnatal depression

Postnatal depression is a type of depression that many parents experience after having a baby.

Read more

Get help with NHS Talking Therapies

NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) offers free, confidential talking therapies on the NHS, including cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), counselling and guided self-help.

You don't need a referral from your GP — you can refer yourself directly.

  • Available to anyone aged 18 or over registered with a GP in England
  • Help for depression, anxiety, panic, phobias, PTSD and more
  • Sessions available in person, by phone or online

Find a service near you

Enter your postcode to find NHS Talking Therapies in your area

Support for under-18s

Mental health support is available specifically for children, teenagers and young adults.

Talk to a parent, carer, teacher or your GP — or use one of the services on the right.

YoungMinds

Parents helpline and online resources for young people

Kooth

Free, safe, anonymous online support for young people

CAMHS

Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services — referral information

Support for carers

Caring for someone with a mental health condition can be rewarding, but can also be hard work. Looking after your own wellbeing is important.

Tips for caring for yourself while caring for others:

  • Take regular breaks — even short ones can help
  • Stay connected with friends and family
  • Keep up with hobbies and activities you enjoy
  • Talk to your GP if you're struggling with low mood
  • Apply for a free carer's assessment from your local council

Read more about looking after yourself as a carer ›

Carers UK helpline

Free expert advice and information for unpaid carers.

0808 808 7777

Monday to Friday, 9am to 6pm

Visit Carers UK website ›
